title: The upper room (Mark 14:12–25)
hookLine: take, this is my body; this is my blood of the covenant
last: SHE HAS DONE A BEAUTIFUL THING.

lines: FOLLOW THE MAN WITH THE WATER JAR.
cards: It's the day the Passover lambs are sacrificed, and the disciples ask: where do you want us to prepare the meal? His instructions sound like a spy novel. Go into the city.
You'll meet a man carrying a pitcher of water. Follow him. Wherever he goes in, ask the owner for the guest room, and he'll show you a large upper room, furnished and ready.
They find it just as he said. That evening, the twelve recline at the table with him. While they eat, he says it: one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me.
They grow sad, and one by one they ask: "Is it I?"

teach.b: Nobody points at anyone else. Each one wonders about himself. Then he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them.

teach.h: TAKE, EAT: THIS IS MY BODY.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Take, eat: this is my body."
He takes a cup, gives thanks, they all drink from it, and he says: "This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many." That word testament is today's word.
In Greek it's diathēkē, and it can mean covenant: a binding agreement. It's why the two halves of the Christian Bible are called the Old and New Testaments, the old and new covenants.
At Mount Sinai, Moses sprinkled blood on the people and called it the blood of the covenant. At a Passover meal, the feast of freedom from Egypt, Jesus takes those words onto his own lips.
Then he says he won't drink wine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God. Christians have gathered around this meal ever since, understanding it in different ways.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine truly become his body and blood. Lutherans say he is truly present in, with and under them.
Many Reformed Christians speak of a real spiritual presence, and many Baptist and other churches keep it as a memorial.

teach.h: THIS IS MY BLOOD OF THE NEW TESTAMENT, WHICH IS SHED FOR MANY.
teach.b: They call it the Eucharist, from the Greek for gave thanks, the Mass, the Divine Liturgy, Holy Communion, the Lord's Supper. And in Mark, over the bread, four verbs: took, blessed, broke, gave.

how: Christians celebrate this meal as the Eucharist, Mass, Divine Liturgy, Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, some daily, some weekly, some monthly, repeating Jesus's words over bread and wine; churches differ in how they understand Christ's presence in it.

games.q: you're at the table. he says: one of you eating with me will betray me. what do the disciples do?
games.why: one by one they ask, "Is it I?" nobody points at anyone else. then he takes bread: "Take, eat: this is my body."

practice: Hold a piece of bread or a cracker if you have one, or picture the next thing you'll eat, and move slowly through the four verbs: take it, give thanks, break it, share it or eat it, thinking of the people who grew it, baked it, carried it.
This isn't communion, just a meal eaten with thanks. If you pray, you can give thanks to God before you eat.

wordCard.voice: Covenant. In Greek, diathēkē: a binding promise, and the old English word testament. The new covenant, in a cup.
